title: Class 10 · Some Applications of Trigonometry — Chapter Test 9

questions.q: A wire is attached from a point $A$ on the ground to the top of a pole $BC$, making an angle of elevation of $60°$. If $AB = 5\sqrt{3}$ m, then the length of the wire is:
questions.solution:
Draw it: $B$ is the foot of the pole, $C$ its top, $A$ the point on the ground. The wire $AC$ is the **hypotenuse**, $AB$ the side **adjacent** to the $60°$ angle at $A$.

Adjacent and hypotenuse means cosine:

$\cos 60° = \dfrac{AB}{AC}$

$\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{AC}$

$AC = 2 \times 5\sqrt{3} = \mathbf{10\sqrt{3}}$ m

The height of the pole, if you wanted it, would be $BC = AB\tan 60° = 5\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} = 15$ m — which is option (D), there to catch anyone who solves for the wrong side.

Before choosing a ratio, name the three sides against the angle you are given: opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse. Which two the question mentions decides whether you need sine, cosine or tangent.

questions.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point on the ground, which is 30 m away from the foot of the tower, is $45°$. The height of the tower is:
questions.solution:
The height is **opposite** the angle and the 30 m is **adjacent**, so use tangent:

$\tan 45° = \dfrac{h}{30}$

$1 = \dfrac{h}{30} \Rightarrow h = \mathbf{30}$ m

An elevation of exactly $45°$ is worth recognising on sight: $\tan 45° = 1$, so the height and the horizontal distance are **equal**. The triangle is isosceles.

Use it as a sanity check on harder problems too — if an angle is bigger than $45°$ the height beats the distance, and if it is smaller the distance wins.

questions.q: If the length of the shadow of a tower on level ground is $\sqrt{3}$ times the height of the tower, the angle of elevation of the Sun is:
questions.solution:
Let the height be $h$; then the shadow is $\sqrt{3}h$.

$\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{shadow}} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}h} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

The acute angle with tangent $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ is $\mathbf{30°}$.

The picture makes it memorable: a **long** shadow means the Sun is **low** in the sky. The shadow here is longer than the tower, so the angle must be less than $45°$ — and $30°$ is the only option below it.

The reverse case is worth knowing too: a shadow $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ times the height means the Sun is at $60°$, high overhead and casting a short shadow.

questions.q: From the top of a lighthouse 60 m high, the angle of depression of a boat is $30°$. The distance of the boat from the foot of the lighthouse is:
questions.solution:
**First, move the angle.** The angle of depression is measured from the *horizontal at the top*, looking down. The horizontal at the top and the ground are parallel, so by alternate angles the angle of **elevation** of the lighthouse top from the boat is also $30°$.

Now, with $d$ the distance along the ground:

$\tan 30° = \dfrac{60}{d}$

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{60}{d} \Rightarrow d = \mathbf{60\sqrt{3}}$ m

The single most common error in this whole chapter is marking the angle of depression *inside* the triangle at the top. It is not there — it sits above the line of sight, between it and the horizontal. Slide it down to the boat and the triangle becomes ordinary.

A check: $30°$ is a shallow angle, so the boat should be far away — $60\sqrt{3} \approx 104$ m against a 60 m height. That feels right.

questions.q: A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground 20 m away from its foot, the angle of elevation of the top is $60°$. The height of the tower is:
questions.solution:
$\tan 60° = \dfrac{h}{20}$

$\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{h}{20} \Rightarrow h = \mathbf{20\sqrt{3}}$ m $\approx 34.6$ m

Option (B) is the same numbers with the fraction upside down — what you get by writing $\tan 60° = \dfrac{20}{h}$. Deciding *which* side is opposite the angle before writing the ratio prevents it.

The angle is above $45°$, so the tower must be **taller** than the 20 m distance. $20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.6$ m passes that test; $\tfrac{20}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 11.5$ m does not.

questions.q: If the angle of elevation of the top of a pole from a point on the ground equals the height of the pole in metres divided by the distance in metres, and that ratio is $1$, the angle is:
questions.solution:
The ratio $\dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}}$ is exactly $\tan\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle of elevation.

$\tan\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = \mathbf{45°}$

This is the case where the triangle is isosceles: the pole is as tall as the observer is far from it.

It is worth fixing the three benchmarks in your head as a ladder:

$\tan 30° = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.58$ — height less than distance

$\tan 45° = 1$ — height equals distance

$\tan 60° = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73$ — height greater than distance

With those, you can often eliminate three options before doing any arithmetic.

questions.q:
A ladder 10 m long rests against a vertical wall, making an angle of $60°$ with the ground. How high up the wall does the ladder reach, in metres?

Give your answer correct to two decimal places. (Use $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$)
questions.solution:
The ladder is the **hypotenuse** (10 m) and the height up the wall is **opposite** the $60°$ angle, so use sine:

$\sin 60° = \dfrac{h}{10}$

$\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{h}{10}$

$h = 10 \times \dfrac{1.732}{2} = \mathbf{8.66}$ m

The foot of the ladder, if asked, would be $10\cos 60° = 5$ m from the wall — and a quick check: $8.66^{2} + 5^{2} = 75 + 25 = 100 = 10^{2}$ ✓ Pythagoras agrees.

A ladder question is always the same triangle. The ladder is the hypotenuse; height and distance-from-wall are the two legs. Which ratio you need depends only on which of the three the question names.

questions.q: From the top of a building 15 m high, the angle of depression of a point on the ground is $45°$. Find the distance of that point from the base of the building, in metres.
questions.solution:
The angle of depression from the top is $45°$, so by alternate angles the angle of **elevation** from the point is also $45°$.

$\tan 45° = \dfrac{15}{d}$

$1 = \dfrac{15}{d} \Rightarrow d = \mathbf{15}$ m

At $45°$ the height and the horizontal distance are always equal — the line of sight is the diagonal of a square. No calculation is really needed once you spot the angle.

Remember the alternate-angles step even here, where the arithmetic is trivial. In the exam it is a mark, and in harder problems it is the step that makes the triangle solvable at all.

questions.topic: Height of a tower from two positions
questions.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point on the ground is $30°$. On walking 40 m towards the tower, the angle becomes $60°$. Find the height of the tower. (Use $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$)
questions.solution:
**Set up.** Let the height be $h$ and let the *nearer* point be $x$ m from the foot. The farther point is then $(x + 40)$ m away.

**Nearer point** ($60°$):

$\tan 60° = \dfrac{h}{x} \Rightarrow h = x\sqrt{3}$ … (1)

**Farther point** ($30°$):

$\tan 30° = \dfrac{h}{x + 40} \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{x + 40}{\sqrt{3}}$ … (2)

**Equate:**

$x\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{x + 40}{\sqrt{3}}$

$3x = x + 40$

$2x = 40 \Rightarrow x = 20$

**Height:**

$h = 20\sqrt{3} = 20 \times 1.732 = \mathbf{34.64}$ m

**Check** with the $30°$ triangle: $\dfrac{60}{\sqrt{3}} = 20\sqrt{3} = 34.64$ ✓

The habit that makes these easy: put the unknown $x$ on the **nearer** distance and write the farther one as $x + 40$. Doing it the other way round works too, but you end up subtracting and it is easier to slip a sign.

questions.q: A tree breaks due to a storm and the broken part bends so that the top of the tree touches the ground, making an angle of $30°$ with it. The distance from the foot of the tree to the point where the top touches the ground is 8 m. Find the height of the tree. (Use $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$)
questions.solution:
**Picture it.** The tree snaps at a point $B$ above the ground. The upper part bends over and its tip touches the ground at $C$, 8 m from the foot $A$. So the standing stump $AB$ and the fallen part $BC$ together make the original tree.

The triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $A$, with the $30°$ angle at $C$.

**The standing part** $AB$ is opposite the $30°$ angle:

$\tan 30° = \dfrac{AB}{8} \Rightarrow AB = \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{3} \approx 4.62$ m

**The broken part** $BC$ is the hypotenuse:

$\cos 30° = \dfrac{8}{BC} \Rightarrow BC = \dfrac{8}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} = \dfrac{16}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{16\sqrt{3}}{3} \approx 9.24$ m

**Total height of the tree** is the two parts added:

$AB + BC = \dfrac{8\sqrt{3}}{3} + \dfrac{16\sqrt{3}}{3} = \dfrac{24\sqrt{3}}{3} = 8\sqrt{3} \approx \mathbf{13.86}$ m

The trap is answering with just the stump, or just the fallen part. **The tree was as tall as both pieces together** — nothing was lost when it broke, it only folded over.

**Check:** $4.62^{2} + 8^{2} = 21.3 + 64 = 85.3$ and $9.24^{2} = 85.4$ ✓ Pythagoras agrees.

questions.topic: Speed from two angles of elevation
questions.q: The angle of elevation of an aircraft from a point $A$ on the ground is $60°$. After a flight of 30 seconds, the angle of elevation changes to $30°$. The aircraft is flying at a constant height of $3500\sqrt{3}$ m at a uniform speed. Find the speed of the aircraft.
questions.solution:
**Set up.** Let the aircraft be at $P$ first and at $Q$ thirty seconds later, both at height $h = 3500\sqrt{3}$ m. Let $B$ and $C$ be the points directly below them.

**First position**, elevation $60°$:

$\tan 60° = \dfrac{h}{AB} \Rightarrow AB = \dfrac{3500\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}} = 3500$ m

**Second position**, elevation $30°$:

$\tan 30° = \dfrac{h}{AC} \Rightarrow AC = 3500\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} = 10500$ m

**Distance flown** is the difference:

$BC = AC - AB = 10500 - 3500 = 7000$ m

**Speed:**

$\text{speed} = \dfrac{7000 \text{ m}}{30 \text{ s}} = \dfrac{700}{3} \text{ m/s} \approx 233.33$ m/s

In km/h: $\dfrac{700}{3} \times \dfrac{18}{5} = \mathbf{840}$ km/h.

The two triangles share the point $A$ and have the same height, so the aircraft's path is the **difference of the two ground distances** — never the sum. Drawing both triangles on the same baseline, with $B$ between $A$ and $C$, makes that obvious and is worth the thirty seconds it takes.

Notice also why $3500\sqrt{3}$ was chosen as the height: it makes both divisions come out whole.

questions.topic: Time from two angles of depression
questions.q: A man on a cliff observes a boat at an angle of depression of $30°$, approaching the shore to the point immediately beneath the observer with uniform speed. Six minutes later, the angle of depression of the boat is found to be $60°$. Find the time taken by the boat to reach the shore from there.
questions.solution:
**Set up.** Let the cliff have height $h$, with the observer at the top and $O$ the point at its foot (the shore point the boat is heading for). Let the boat be at $P$ first and at $Q$ six minutes later.

By alternate angles, the elevations from $P$ and $Q$ are $30°$ and $60°$.

**First position:**

$\tan 30° = \dfrac{h}{OP} \Rightarrow OP = h\sqrt{3}$

**Second position:**

$\tan 60° = \dfrac{h}{OQ} \Rightarrow OQ = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$

**Distance covered in 6 minutes:**

$PQ = OP - OQ = h\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{3h - h}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{2h}{\sqrt{3}}$

**Distance still to go:** $OQ = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$

**Compare them.** The speed is uniform, so time is proportional to distance:

$\dfrac{\text{time remaining}}{6} = \dfrac{OQ}{PQ} = \dfrac{h/\sqrt{3}}{2h/\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$\text{time remaining} = \mathbf{3}$ minutes.

The height $h$ cancels — and that is the elegance of the question. You are never told the height of the cliff and you never need it, because only the *ratio* of the two distances matters.

Whenever a problem gives you a time for one stretch and asks for the time on another, look for that cancellation before reaching for numbers.

questions.q: A girl 1.5 m tall is standing at some distance from a 30 m high tower. The angle of elevation from her eye to the top of the tower increases from $30°$ to $60°$ as she walks towards the tower. Find the distance she walked towards the tower.
questions.solution:
**Account for her height first.** Her eyes are 1.5 m above the ground, so the tower rises only

$30 - 1.5 = 28.5$ m

above her line of sight. That $28.5$ is the height in every triangle below.

**Far position**, elevation $30°$:

$\tan 30° = \dfrac{28.5}{d_1} \Rightarrow d_1 = 28.5\sqrt{3}$

**Near position**, elevation $60°$:

$\tan 60° = \dfrac{28.5}{d_2} \Rightarrow d_2 = \dfrac{28.5}{\sqrt{3}}$

**Distance walked:**

$d_1 - d_2 = 28.5\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{28.5}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{28.5 \times 3 - 28.5}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{57}{\sqrt{3}} = 19\sqrt{3}$

$= 19 \times 1.732 \approx \mathbf{32.9}$ m

The step that separates full marks from partial is the **1.5 m**. The angles are measured from her *eye*, not her feet, so the triangle's vertical side is $28.5$ m and not $30$. Subtract the observer's height at the very start and the rest is the standard two-triangle calculation.

(Her horizontal distance from the tower does not change by her height — only the vertical side does.)

questions.topic: A kite seen from two points
questions.q: A kite is flying at a height of 60 m above the ground. Ravi, standing on the roof of a house, holds the string straight and observes the angle of elevation of the kite as $30°$. From the bottom of the same building, the angle of elevation of the kite is $45°$. Find the length of the string and the height of the roof from the ground. (Use $\sqrt{3} = 1.73$)
questions.solution:
**From the bottom of the building** ($45°$, full height 60 m):

$\tan 45° = \dfrac{60}{d} \Rightarrow d = 60$ m

where $d$ is the horizontal distance from the building to the point below the kite. This is the same horizontal distance for Ravi on the roof.

**From the roof** ($30°$). Let the roof be $r$ m above the ground; the kite is then $(60 - r)$ m above Ravi:

$\tan 30° = \dfrac{60 - r}{60}$

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{60 - r}{60}$

$60 - r = \dfrac{60}{\sqrt{3}} = 20\sqrt{3} = 20 \times 1.73 = 34.6$

$r = 60 - 34.6 = \mathbf{25.4}$ m — the height of the roof.

**Length of the string.** The string is the hypotenuse of Ravi's triangle, with $(60 - r)$ opposite the $30°$ angle:

$\sin 30° = \dfrac{60 - r}{\text{string}} \Rightarrow \text{string} = \dfrac{34.6}{0.5} = \mathbf{69.2}$ m

(Exactly, the string is $40\sqrt{3} \approx 69.28$ m and the roof is $60 - 20\sqrt{3} \approx 25.36$ m.)

**Check:** the string's horizontal component is $69.2\cos 30° = 69.2 \times 0.865 = 59.9 \approx 60$ ✓ — the same $d$ the first triangle gave.

The link between the two triangles is that **shared horizontal distance**. Find it from the easy $45°$ triangle first, then carry it into the harder one.

questions.topic: Two pillars either side of a road
questions.q: Two pillars of equal lengths stand on either side of a road which is 100 m wide, exactly opposite to each other. At a point on the road between the pillars, the angles of elevation of the tops of the pillars are $60°$ and $30°$. Find the length of each pillar and the distance of the point on the road from the pillars. (Use $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$)
questions.solution:
**Set up.** Let the two pillars each have height $h$, and let the point be $x$ m from the foot of the first pillar. Then it is $(100 - x)$ m from the second.

**Towards the nearer pillar** ($60°$):

$\tan 60° = \dfrac{h}{x} \Rightarrow h = x\sqrt{3}$ … (1)

**Towards the farther pillar** ($30°$):

$\tan 30° = \dfrac{h}{100 - x} \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{100 - x}{\sqrt{3}}$ … (2)

**Equate (1) and (2)** — this is the step that uses "equal lengths":

$x\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{100 - x}{\sqrt{3}}$

$3x = 100 - x$

$4x = 100 \Rightarrow x = 25$

So the point is **25 m** from one pillar and $100 - 25 = $ **75 m** from the other.

**Height:**

$h = 25\sqrt{3} = 25 \times 1.732 = \mathbf{43.3}$ m

**Check** with the other triangle: $\dfrac{75}{\sqrt{3}} = 25\sqrt{3} = 43.3$ ✓

Two unknowns, $h$ and $x$, and two triangles — so two equations. The phrase "of equal lengths" is what lets you set the two expressions for $h$ equal to each other; without it the problem would not be solvable.

Steeper angle, nearer pillar: $60°$ gives 25 m and $30°$ gives 75 m, exactly as the picture suggests.
